inline.s: The Buddha told Ananda: “Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, is boundless in majestic power. In the worlds of the ten directions, the immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable Buddhas and Tathagatas all praise him. In the eastern direction, in Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, immeasurable and countless bodhisattvas all journey to where the Buddha of Immeasurable Life dwells, to revere and make offerings to him and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers, to listen to and receive the sutras and Dharma, and to proclaim the teaching of the Way. In the southern, western, and northern directions, and in the four intermediate directions, above and below, it is likewise so.”
Then the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
In Buddha-lands of the east, their number like the Ganges’ sands, the bodhisattvas of those lands go to behold the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment.
South, west, and north, the four intermediate directions, above and below as well: the bodhisattvas of those lands go to behold the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment.
All those bodhisattvas each bring heavenly wondrous flowers, precious incense, and priceless garments, to make offerings to the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment.
All together they play heavenly music, pouring forth harmonious and elegant sounds, singing in praise of the most supreme Honored One, making offerings to the Buddha of Immeasurable Enlightenment.
Fully penetrating the wisdom of spiritual powers, they enter the profound Dharma-gates; complete in the treasury of merit, their wondrous wisdom has no equal.
The sun of wisdom lights up the world, dispelling the clouds of birth and death; reverently they circle three times and bow their heads to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Seeing that adorned Pure Land, subtle and inconceivable, they accordingly bring forth the immeasurable mind—may my land be likewise.
Then the Honored One of Immeasurable Life changed countenance and gave a joyful smile; from his mouth came countless rays of light, illumining the lands of the ten directions.
The light returned and circled his body, then after three circuits entered at the crown of his head; all the assemblies of devas and humans leaped up and rejoiced.
The great being Avalokiteshvara, adjusting his robes, bowed his head and asked, addressing the Buddha: for what reason do you smile? Pray, tell us your meaning.
The Brahma-voice is like thunder; the eight tones pour forth wondrous sound. I shall bestow the bodhisattva prediction; now I speak—listen well, good sir.
Upright men who come from the ten directions—I know all their vows: they aspire to adorn the Pure Land and, having received the prophecy, shall become Buddhas.
Awakening to all dharmas as like a dream, an illusion, an echo, they fulfill all their wondrous vows and shall surely accomplish such a land.
Knowing dharmas to be like lightning flashes, they perfect the bodhisattva way; with all the roots of their merit, having received the prophecy, they shall become Buddhas.
Penetrating the nature of all dharmas, all is empty and without self; with wisdom they seek the pure Buddha-land and shall surely accomplish such a land.
The Buddhas tell the bodhisattvas: now go and behold the Buddha of Peace and Nourishment; hearing the Dharma, take joy in practicing it, and swiftly attain the land of purity.
Arriving in that adorned and purified land, they will swiftly gain spiritual powers, and before the Honored One of Immeasurable Life they will receive the prophecy and accomplish equal enlightenment.
By the power of that Buddha’s original vows, those who hear his name and wish to be reborn all reach that land and of themselves attain irreversibility.
Bodhisattvas bring forth the highest vow—may my land be without difference—and universally resolve to save all beings; their fame shines throughout the ten directions.
Serving a hundred million Tathagatas, flying in transformation to every land, reverently and joyfully they depart and return again to the Land of Peace and Nourishment.
If a person has no good mind, he cannot hear this sutra; only the pure who keep the precepts may hear the right Dharma.
Those who have met the World-Honored One before can believe this matter; humble and reverent, they hear and practice it, leaping up in great joy.
The proud, the mean, and the indolent find it hard to believe this Dharma; those who have seen the Buddhas in former lives delight in hearing such a teaching.
Hearers or bodhisattvas cannot fathom the saintly mind; it is as with one born blind who would lead and guide others.
The Tathagata’s ocean of wisdom is deep and vast, without shore or bottom; the two vehicles cannot fathom it—only a Buddha alone understands it clearly.
Suppose all people were complete in having attained the Way, with pure wisdom like original emptiness, and for a million kalpas pondered the Buddha’s wisdom—
exhausting their powers and expounding it to the utmost, to the end of life they still would not know it; the Buddha’s wisdom has no bound—thus does one attain purity.
A human lifespan is most hard to obtain, and a Buddha’s world most hard to meet; that people have faith and wisdom is hard—if you hear, strive on and seek.
Hearing the Dharma, able to hold it in mind and, seeing and revering it, gaining great celebration—such a one is my good friend; therefore you should set your mind on it.
Though the whole world were filled with fire, one must pass through it to hear the Dharma; one will surely accomplish the Buddha-way and broadly rescue the stream of birth and death.
Verses on Going to Behold

The Buddha told Ananda: “The bodhisattvas in that land shall all ultimately reach the stage of one lifetime from Buddhahood, except those whose original vows, for the sake of living beings, adorn themselves with the merit of their great vows, wishing universally to save and release all living beings. Ananda, among the hearers in that Buddha’s land, the bodily radiance of each is one fathom; the radiance of the bodhisattvas shines for a hundred yojanas. There are two bodhisattvas, most honored and foremost, whose majestic radiance illumines three thousand great thousand worlds.”

Ananda said to the Buddha: “What are the names of those two bodhisattvas?” The Buddha said: “One is named Avalokiteshvara, the second is named Mahasthamaprapta. These two bodhisattvas cultivated the bodhisattva practice in this land, and when their lives ended they were transformed and born in that Buddha’s land. Ananda, all living beings born in that land are complete in the thirty-two marks, fulfilled in wisdom, deeply entering all dharmas, thoroughly penetrating the essential and wondrous, unobstructed in spiritual powers, with clear and keen faculties. Those of dull faculties accomplish the two forbearances; those of keen faculties attain the incalculable forbearance of the non-arising of dharmas. Moreover, those bodhisattvas, until they become Buddhas, do not undergo evil destinies; sovereign in spiritual powers, they always know their past lives. They are excepted only if born in another region of the five turbid evil worlds, where they manifest like those there, as in my own land.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “The bodhisattvas in that land, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic power, in the time of a single meal journey to the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and reverently make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Whatever their minds conceive—flowers and incense, music, garments and canopies, banners and pennants, and offerings immeasurable and countless—arises by transformation of itself and arrives as soon as thought of. Rare, wondrous, and surpassing, such as the world does not possess, they scatter them in offering before the Buddhas and the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers. In the sky they transform into flower canopies, blazing with light and color, their fragrance pervading all. Where those flowers are four hundred li around, in like manner doubling again and again, they cover three thousand great thousand worlds, and following one after another they vanish by transformation. All those bodhisattvas, rejoicing together, in the sky join in heavenly music and with subtle and wondrous sounds sing in praise of the Buddha’s virtues; hearing and receiving the sutras and Dharma, their joy is immeasurable. Having made offerings to the Buddha, before they have eaten, they suddenly rise lightly and return to their own land.”

The Buddha said to Ananda: “When Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, proclaims the Dharma to the hearers, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans, they all gather in the Hall of the Seven Treasures, where he broadly proclaims the teaching of the Way and unfolds the wondrous Dharma; none fails to rejoice, and their minds open in understanding and attain the Way. At once winds arise naturally from the four quarters, blowing on the trees of the seven treasures and bringing forth the five tones. Immeasurable wondrous flowers scatter with the wind in every direction, making offerings of themselves, and so without cease. All the devas each bring hundreds of thousands of heavenly flowers and incenses and ten thousand kinds of music, making offerings to that Buddha and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers. They scatter flowers and incense everywhere and play all kinds of music, coming and going back and forth, each making way for the other; at such a time their joy and delight cannot be fully told.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Whatever the bodhisattvas born in that Buddha’s land expound, they always proclaim the right Dharma, in accord with wisdom, without transgression or loss. Toward all things in that land they have no mind of ‘mine,’ no mind of defilement. In coming and going, advancing and resting, their feelings are tied to nothing. According to their wish they are sovereign, without preference or aversion; without ‘that’ or ‘I,’ without contention or dispute. Toward all living beings they gain a mind of great compassion and beneficence. Soft and tamed, they have no mind of hatred. Apart from the coverings, they are pure, with no mind of weariness or indolence. They have the mind of equality, the mind of victory, the mind of profundity, the mind of concentration, and the mind that loves, delights in, and rejoices in the Dharma. They extinguish all afflictions and are free of the mind of evil destinies. They fulfill all the practices of the bodhisattvas and are complete in accomplishing immeasurable merit. They attain profound meditative concentration, all penetrations and clear wisdom, and roam in aspiration through the seven factors of enlightenment, cultivating the mind of the Buddha-Dharma.

With the fleshly eye, clear and pure, nothing is not distinctly seen; with the divine eye, penetrating, immeasurable and boundless; with the Dharma-eye, observing, they fathom all paths; with the wisdom-eye, seeing the truth, they can cross to the other shore; with the Buddha-eye, complete, they awaken to the nature of dharmas and, with unobstructed wisdom, expound the Dharma for others. They regard the three realms equally, as empty and nothing at all; they aspire to the Buddha-Dharma, are complete in all eloquence, and extinguish the afflictions that torment living beings. Born from the Tathagata, they understand dharmas as they truly are, and are skilled in knowing the methods of the sound of gathering and cessation. They take no delight in worldly speech but rejoice in right discourse. They cultivate all roots of goodness and aspire to the Buddha-way. Knowing that all dharmas are utterly quiescent, they exhaust both the afflictions of this present body and the residues that remain. Hearing the profound Dharma, their minds feel no doubt or fear. Those who can always practice great compassion are deep, vast, and subtle, bearing and covering all. They reach the ultimate One Vehicle and arrive at the other shore; they cut through the net of doubt, and wisdom issues from the mind.

In the Buddha’s teaching they embrace all without exception; their wisdom is like the great sea, their samadhi like the king of mountains. The light of their wisdom is pure and bright, surpassing the sun and moon. The dharmas of purity are complete and perfect. Like a mountain of clouds, they illumine all merits with a single purity; like the earth, they hold no different mind toward pure or foul, good or bad; like pure water, they wash away all dust and defilement; like the king of fire, they burn up the fuel of every affliction; like a great wind, they move through all worlds without obstruction; like space, they cling to nothing in all existence; like a lotus flower, they are unstained by any world; like a great vehicle, they carry multitudes across birth and death; like thick clouds, they shake the great Dharma-thunder to awaken the unawakened; like abundant rain, they rain the sweet dew of Dharma to nourish living beings; like a diamond mountain, they cannot be shaken by demons or outsiders; like Brahma, they are foremost among all good dharmas; like a banyan tree, they cover all; like an udumbara flower, they are rare and hard to meet; like a golden-winged bird, they subdue outsiders; like flocks of birds, they hoard nothing; like the king of oxen, they are unequaled; like the king of elephants, they are well tamed; like the king of lions, they are fearless; vast as space, they are equal through great compassion; destroying jealousy, they do not begrudge the superior.

They take joy in seeking the Dharma with minds that never tire. They always wish to speak it widely, their resolve never wearying. They beat the Dharma-drum, raise the Dharma-banner, shine the sun of wisdom, and dispel the darkness of delusion. They practice the six harmonies of reverence and always give the gift of Dharma, advancing with courage, their minds never retreating or weakening. They are lamps for the world, the supreme field of merit. They are always teachers and guides, equal without hate or love, delighting only in the right path, with no other joy or grief. They draw out the thorns of desire and bring peace to living beings. Their merits are supreme; all revere them. They extinguish the three defilements and course in spiritual powers. They possess the powers of cause, condition, intention, vow, and skillful means; the powers of constancy, goodness, concentration, insight, and much hearing; the powers of giving, precepts, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom; the powers of right mindfulness, calm and insight, and all penetrations and clarity; and the Tathagata’s power of taming living beings. All such powers are complete in them. Their bodily form and marks, their merits and eloquence are complete and adorned, unequaled by any. They revere and make offerings to countless Buddhas and are always praised by all Buddhas together. They fulfill the bodhisattva paramitas and cultivate the samadhis of emptiness, marklessness, and wishlessness, and the samadhi-gates of non-arising and non-ceasing, far removed from the stages of hearers and solitary buddhas. Ananda, those bodhisattvas accomplish such immeasurable merits; I have spoken of them only in brief for you. Were I to speak in full, a hundred thousand million kalpas could not exhaust them.”

The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of devas and humans: “In the land of Immeasurable Life, the hearers and bodhisattvas, their merits and wisdom, cannot be described. Moreover, that land is so subtle and blissful, so pure as this—why do you not strive to do good? Think on the naturalness of the Way. Abide in neither high nor low, penetrate without limit; each should strive diligently and seek it for yourselves. You will surely pass beyond and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, cutting across the five evil paths; the roads of rebirth close of themselves. Ascend the Way without end—easy to go, yet none go; that land does not oppose or reject, drawn by naturalness. Why not abandon worldly affairs and diligently practice the Way and its virtue? You may attain the utmost long life, with bliss without end.

Yet worldly people are shallow and vulgar, contending together over what is not urgent, and amid this fierce evil and extreme suffering they labor body and mind to provide for themselves. With no noble or base, no poor or rich, young and old, men and women, all worry over wealth; the having and the not having are the same, their anxious thoughts equal. They fret and sorrow, piling up cares and schemes. Driven by the mind, they have no hour of peace. Having fields, they worry over fields; having houses, they worry over houses. Cattle, horses, the six kinds of livestock, servants, wealth, clothing, food, and goods—they worry over all of it. With heavy thoughts and ceaseless sighs, they grieve, brood, and dread; and unforeseen calamities come upon them—fire and water, thieves, enemies, creditors—burning, drowning, seizing, plundering, scattering and destroying them. The poison of care leaves them dazed, with no hour of release. Resentment knots within the heart, never parting from grief and vexation. The mind is hard and the will fixed, with no letting go. Or they sit and are crushed; body dies and life ends, and they are cast away and gone, with none to follow. The noble and wealthy have this affliction too, with ten thousand anxieties and fears, toiling and suffering like this, accumulating all manner of chills and fevers, dwelling together with pain. The poor and lowly, pressed by want, are always without. Having no fields, they worry and wish for fields; having no houses, they worry and wish for houses; having no cattle, horses, livestock, servants, wealth, clothing, food, or goods, they worry and wish to have them. Just as they have one thing, they lack another; having this and lacking that, they think of making them equal. Just as they would have them all, they are scattered again. Thus in grief and toil they must seek anew, and cannot always obtain; their thoughts bring no benefit, and body and mind both labor, unable to sit or rise in peace, with anxious thoughts following after. Toiling and suffering like this, they also accumulate all manner of chills and fevers, dwelling together with pain; or in time they sit and meet an early death, unwilling to do good, to practice the Way, or to advance in virtue. When their lifespan ends and they die, they must go far alone, heading toward some destination, on the paths of good and evil, and none can know it.

Between people of the world—father and son, elder and younger brother, husband and wife, household and family, kin within and without—there should be mutual respect and love, with no mutual hatred or envy. Sharing what they have, they should not be greedy or grudging; their words and looks should always be gentle, never contrary or harsh. Yet sometimes, though the mind be calm, anger arises; the resentment of this life, with the slightest mutual hatred and envy, grows fiercer in later lives, until it becomes great enmity. Why is this? In the affairs of the world, people bring harm to one another; though not immediately, they should at once dissolve it. But they harbor poison and store up anger, knotting resentment in the spirit; naturally it is marked and known, and they cannot be parted from it. They must be born facing one another, each taking revenge on the other. People in the world, amid love and desire, are born alone and die alone, go alone and come alone. When they come to the places of suffering and bliss according to their bent, they must bear it themselves, and there is none to take their place. Good and evil transform, and calamity and blessing occupy different places; prepared and waiting from of old, they must enter alone, going far to another place where none can see them. Good and evil come naturally, following where one is born; dark and hidden, parted for long, their roads differ and meeting has no set time. It is very hard, very hard, to meet now as we have. Why not abandon all affairs, and while each is still strong and well, strive diligently to cultivate goodness and advance with vigor, vowing to cross over the world and attain the utmost long life? Why do you not seek the Way? What are you waiting for? What pleasure do you seek? Such worldly people do not believe that doing good brings good and practicing the Way brings the Way; they do not believe that people die and are reborn, or that giving brings blessing. The affairs of good and evil they do not believe at all, saying it is not so, that in the end there is no such thing. Only because of this, and seeing it for themselves, they look at one another, and former and latter are the same. Passing it on in turn, by the leftover commands of fathers, the ancestors of old never did good and did not know the Way and its virtue; dull in body and dark in spirit, their minds blocked and their thoughts shut. The destinies of death and birth, the paths of good and evil, they cannot see for themselves, and there is none to tell them. Good and ill fortune, calamity and blessing, they vie to bring about, and none finds it strange. The constant way of birth and death passes on in turn; or a father weeps for a son, or a son weeps for a father, brothers, husbands and wives weep for one another. Upside down and inverted, the root of impermanence—all must pass away and cannot be kept forever. They teach and guide, but few believe; thus birth and death flow on without rest. People such as these, benighted and obstinate, do not believe the sutras and Dharma; their minds take no far thought, each wishing only for present pleasure, deluded by craving and desire, not reaching the Way and its virtue, lost and drowned in anger, greedy as wolves for wealth and lust. Because of this they do not attain the Way, and must undergo still more suffering in evil destinies; birth and death have no end—alas, how pitiable!

Or sometimes within a household, father and son, brothers, husband and wife, one dies and one lives, and they grieve for one another. With love and longing, their thoughts bound and tied, their minds aching and clinging, they look back on one another day after day and year after year, with no release. They are taught the Way and its virtue, but their minds do not open; they dwell on affection and fondness, never leaving desire. Dull and benighted, blocked and shut, covered by delusion, they cannot think deeply or plan well, set their minds upright, and single-mindedly practice the Way, cutting off worldly affairs. So they spin on to the end, and when their years and life are spent they cannot attain the Way, and there is no help for it. All are muddled and restless, all greedy for love and desire. Those deluded about the Way are many, those who awaken few; the world hurries on, with nothing to rely on. Noble and base, high and low, rich and poor, honored and humble, all toil and bustle, each harboring murderous poison. Evil airs are dark and hidden, and they raise affairs in delusion, opposing Heaven and Earth, not following the human heart. Natural evil is not theirs—first it follows and gives to them, indulging what they do, awaiting the fullness of their guilt. Before their lifespan ends, it suddenly seizes them away. They fall into evil destinies, toiling through life after life, turning and turning within them for thousands of millions of kalpas, with no time of escape. The pain is beyond words—how pitiable!”

The Buddha told Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assembly of devas and humans: “I now tell you: in the affairs of the world, because of this people sit and do not attain the Way. You should think carefully and plan, and keep far from all evil. Choose what is good and practice it diligently. Love, desire, glory, and splendor cannot be kept forever; all must be parted from, and there is nothing to delight in. Meeting a Buddha in the world, you should strive with vigor. Those who with the utmost vow seek birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss may attain wisdom and clarity, and merits supreme. Do not follow the desires of your mind, failing and betraying the sutras and precepts, falling behind others. If any have doubts and do not understand the sutras, let them ask the Buddha fully, and he will explain it to them.”

Maitreya Bodhisattva, kneeling long, said: “The Buddha’s majesty and honor are revered; what you have spoken is excellent and good. Hearing the Buddha’s sutra words and pondering them through the mind, worldly people are indeed so, as the Buddha has said. Now the Buddha in compassion reveals the great Way, opening eyes and ears, so that we may long be freed. Hearing what the Buddha has said, none fails to rejoice. All the devas, humans, and crawling creatures receive your compassionate grace and are released from grief and suffering. The Buddha’s words of instruction and precept are most profound and good; his wisdom clearly sees the affairs of the eight directions, above and below, past, future, and present, and nothing is left unpenetrated. That we in this assembly have been freed is due to the Buddha’s humble toil when he sought the Way in former lives. His grace and virtue cover all; his blessings tower high, his light shines through, reaching emptiness without limit, opening for people nirvana. His teaching and guidance, his authority and transformation—he moves the ten directions without end. The Buddha is the Dharma King, honored beyond all sages, the teacher of all devas and humans, and according to the wishes of their minds he brings them all to the Way. Now to meet the Buddha and again hear the name of Immeasurable Life—none fails to rejoice, and their minds open in clarity.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “What you say is so. If any have compassion and reverence for the Buddha, that is truly great goodness. Only after long ages does a Buddha appear in the world again. Now I have become Buddha in this world and expound the sutras and Dharma, proclaim the teaching of the Way, cut the net of doubts, pull out the root of craving, and block up the source of all evil. I walk through the three realms without obstruction. Holding the essentials of wisdom, the key to all paths, I grasp the guiding principles, clear and distinct. I reveal the five destinies and save the unsaved, settling the way of birth and death and nirvana.

Maitreya, you should know that from countless kalpas past you have practiced the bodhisattva path, wishing to save living beings—this for a long time. Those who have attained the Way through you, up to nirvana, cannot be counted. You and all the devas and humans of the ten directions, all the four assemblies, through long kalpas have turned through the five paths, in grief, fear, and toil beyond all telling; even in this present life birth and death have not ceased, yet you have met the Buddha, heard the sutras and Dharma, and again heard of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. How excellent, how good! I share in your joy.

You too may now weary of birth and death and the pains of old age, sickness, and suffering, of the foul and impure, with nothing to delight in. You should decide for yourselves, make your body upright and your conduct correct, and do ever more good. Cultivate yourselves, cleanse your bodies, wash away the defilements of the mind. In word and deed be loyal and trustworthy, outer and inner in accord. People may save themselves and in turn rescue one another, seeking with clarity and keenness and accumulating the roots of goodness. Though this one life be toilsome, in a moment afterward you will be born in the Land of Immeasurable Life of boundless bliss. Long will you be joined in clarity with the Way and virtue, forever pulling out the root of birth and death, with no more affliction of greed, anger, delusion, or sorrow; and if you wish for a lifespan of one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand million myriads of kalpas, freely and at will, all may be obtained. This is actionless and natural, next to the way of nirvana. Each of you should strive, seeking what your mind desires, and not give way to doubt or regret and make fault for yourselves, born in the border region in palaces of the seven treasures, for five hundred years undergoing all manner of adversity.” Maitreya said: “Receiving the Buddha’s weighty instruction, I will single-mindedly study and practice, following the teaching, and dare not have doubt.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “You are able, in this world, to set the mind upright and correct, to do no evil—this is the highest virtue, unequaled in the worlds of the ten directions. Why is that? In the Buddha-lands, devas and humans naturally do good and do not greatly do evil, and are easy to guide. Now I have become Buddha in this world, dwelling amid the five evils, the five pains, and the five burnings, in the most extreme suffering. I teach and transform living beings, leading them to abandon the five evils, to put away the five pains, to leave the five burnings, to subdue and transform their minds, to keep the five goods, to gain their merit and blessing—the way of long life in the world and nirvana.”

The Buddha said: “What are the five evils? What are the five pains? What are the five burnings? How does one transform the five evils, keep the five goods, and gain the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world and nirvana?

First, the evil: devas, humans, and crawling creatures all wish to do evil; the strong overpower the weak, and each in turn injures and kills the other, devouring one another, not knowing how to cultivate goodness, perverse and without the Way. Afterward they receive the punishment of calamity, naturally bent thither. The gods record and know; the offender is not pardoned. Hence there are poverty and lowliness, beggars and the solitary, the deaf, the blind, and the mute, and the foolish, base, and evil—down to the deformed and insane and the deficient. And there are the noble and wealthy, the talented and clear-minded: all this comes from kindness and filial piety in former lives, from cultivating goodness and piling up virtue. There is a constant way in the world: the king’s law and the prisons. Yet they will not fear and be careful, but do evil and fall into crime and receive its punishment; seeking to be released, they hardly escape. Such things are seen now in the world; after death, in later lives, it is deeper and fiercer still. Entering the darkness, they are reborn and receive a body—as with the king’s law, with the utmost pain of torture.

Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering. They trade their bodies, change their forms and their paths; the lifespan they receive is long or short. The spirit and consciousness naturally go thither. Alone they meet their end, and following one another they are born together. Each avenges the other without cease. While their evil is not exhausted, they cannot be parted. Turning and turning within, they have no time of escape, and it is hard to be freed. The pain is beyond words. Between Heaven and Earth this is natural; though it does not fall at once in sudden violence, the way of good and evil will surely come home. This is the first great evil, first pain, first burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and conduct correct, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvana—this is the first great good.”

The Buddha said: “Second, the evil: the people of the world, fathers and sons, brothers, households and couples, are all without righteousness or principle, not following the Dharma and its measure, extravagant, licentious, arrogant, and self-indulgent, each wishing only for present pleasure. They give the mind free rein, each deceiving and deluding the other; mind and mouth differ, and their words are without truth. Flattering and fawning, unfaithful, with clever words and adulation, they envy the worthy and slander the good, ruining and wronging them. When the ruler is unclear and employs his ministers, the ministers do as they please, with endless schemes and falsehoods, overstepping their measure and knowing the state of things; those in office are not upright and are deceived by them, recklessly harming the loyal and good, not according with the heart of Heaven. Ministers deceive their lords, children their fathers, brothers, husbands and wives, relatives and acquaintances deceive one another. Each harbors greed, anger, and delusion; each wishes to enrich himself and craves much. Noble and base, high and low—their minds are all the same. They ruin the family and lose their lives, giving no thought to what comes before or after. Kin within and without are destroyed with them. Or sometimes a household or acquaintance, a village or market quarter, foolish folk and rustics, turn together to such dealings; each harms or profits the other, and anger becomes a knot of resentment. The rich are stingy and will not give; they cling to what they love, their greed heavy, their minds toiling and their bodies suffering. Thus to the very end they have nothing to rely on; they come alone and go alone, with none to follow. Good and evil, calamity and blessing, follow the life where one is born; or they go to a place of bliss, or enter bitter poison—and then they repent. What use is that?

The people of the world, foolish of mind and scant of wisdom, seeing the good they hate and slander them, with no thought of emulating them; they wish only to do evil and recklessly commit what is against the Dharma. Always harboring a thievish mind, coveting others’ gain, they scatter and waste what they have and then seek for more. Their minds are crooked and not upright; they fear that others see them; they take no forethought, and only when the matter comes do they repent.

In this present life there are the king’s laws and prisons; according to their crimes they go and receive their punishment. Because in former lives they did not believe the Way and its virtue, did not cultivate the roots of goodness, and now again do evil, the gods mark and know them and record their names in the ledgers. When their lifespan ends and the spirit departs, they descend into evil destinies. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering; turning and turning within them, life after life, kalpa after kalpa, they have no time of escape, and it is hard to be freed. The pain is beyond words. This is the second great evil, second pain, second burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and conduct correct, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvana—this is the second great good.”

The Buddha said: “Third, the evil: the people of the world, born leaning on one another, dwell together between Heaven and Earth. The years of their lifespan—how many can there be? Above are the wise and noble elders, the honored and wealthy; below are the poor and menial, the feeble and foolish; in the middle are those who are not good. Always harboring evil, thinking only of lust, their breasts full of trouble, their love and desire in confusion, they cannot sit or rise in peace; covetous and stingy, wishing only to gain without effort. They glance sidelong at fine forms, their lewd manner showing without. They loathe and hate their own wives and steal in and out in secret, wasting the family wealth in unlawful deeds. They form ties and gather, raise troops and fight one another, attack and rob and kill, seize by force without the Way. Their evil minds are set on the outside, and they do not cultivate their own work; they steal and snatch what they can, plotting blows to accomplish their ends. By threats and force they gather wealth to give to wife and children, giving the mind free rein and taking their pleasure, indulging the body in delight. Or with their own kin, not avoiding noble or base, in the household within and without, they bring grief and suffering, and also do not fear the king’s law or its prohibitions. Such evil is plain to humans and ghosts; sun and moon shine on it, and the gods record and know. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering; turning and turning within them, life after life, kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape, hard to be freed, the pain beyond words. This is the third great evil, third pain, third burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and conduct correct, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvana—this is the third great good.”

The Buddha said: “Fourth, the evil: the people of the world do not think of cultivating goodness but teach one another and do evil together—two-tongued speech, harsh speech, false speech, and idle speech; slander and treachery, strife and disorder, hating and envying the good, ruining the worthy and clear, taking joy at their side. They are unfilial to their two parents and slight and scorn their teachers and elders; among friends they are without trust and rarely honest. The noble and honored are proud and great, saying they themselves possess the Way; they run wild with power and force and encroach upon others. They cannot know themselves, are shameless in doing evil, think themselves strong and healthy, and wish others to respect and fear them. They do not revere Heaven and Earth, the gods, sun, and moon, and will not do good; they are hard to tame. Self-willed and haughty, they think it can always be so, with no care or fear, always harboring arrogance. Such evils the gods record and know. Because in former lives they did some merit and blessing, and small goodness supported and protected them, in this life they do evil, their merit and blessing are all destroyed, and the good gods and spirits each depart and leave them; they stand alone and empty with nothing to rely on. When their lifespan is spent, all evils return to them; naturally they are pressed and hurried, and together rush to seize them. Their names are recorded with the gods; calamity and guilt draw them on to the place they must go. The retribution of their crimes is natural, with no way to leave it; they can only go forward and enter the cauldron of fire, body and mind crushed, spirit in pain. At such a time, what use is regret? The way of Heaven is clear; there is no stumbling. Hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering; turning and turning within them, life after life, kalpa after kalpa, with no time of escape, hard to be freed, the pain beyond words. This is the fourth great evil, fourth pain, fourth burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and conduct correct, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvana—this is the fourth great good.”

The Buddha said: “Fifth, the evil: the people of the world lean and loiter, indolent and lazy, unwilling to do good, to cultivate the body, or to attend to their work. Their households and kin suffer hunger and cold, and when father and mother teach and admonish them they glare and answer in anger. Their words and commands are not harmonious, but contrary and rebellious, like enemies—better to have had no son. In taking and giving they know no measure, and all alike find them hateful. They betray kindness and violate righteousness, with no thought of repayment. Poor and pressed by want, unable to gain more, they seize by force and plunder, giving themselves up to idleness and roaming. Long accustomed to getting things for nothing to relieve themselves, they are addicted to drink and dote on delicacies, eating and drinking without measure, giving the mind free rein and roaming at ease, rude and obstinate. They do not know human feeling and force their will on others. Seeing others’ good, they hate it with envy. Without righteousness or propriety, with no care or scruple, self-willed and self-approved, they cannot be admonished. For the support of their six kinds of kin they feel no concern. They do not think on the kindness of father and mother, nor keep the righteousness of teacher and friend. Their minds always think evil, their mouths always speak evil, their bodies always do evil; never once a good deed. They do not believe in the sutras and Dharma of the former sages and Buddhas, do not believe that practicing the Way can bring deliverance from the world, do not believe that after death the spirit is reborn, do not believe that doing good brings good and doing evil brings evil. They wish to kill true persons and to set the assembly of monks at strife. They wish to harm father and mother, brothers, and kin. Their six kinds of kin they hate and loathe and wish dead. Such worldly people—their minds and thoughts are all alike, foolish and benighted, yet they think themselves wise. They do not know where they come from in birth, nor where they go in death. Unkind and disobedient, they oppose Heaven and Earth. And amid all this they hope for luck and wish for long life, yet in the end must die. With a compassionate mind one teaches them and makes them think on goodness, reveals birth and death and the destinies of good and evil, and that this is natural—yet they will not believe it. To speak to them with a bitter heart brings them no benefit; their minds are shut and blocked and their thoughts do not open. As the great command of life is about to end, regret and fear come together. They did not cultivate goodness beforehand, and only at the end do they repent. What use is repenting afterward?

Between Heaven and Earth the five paths are clearly divided, vast and dark, broad and boundless. Good and evil bring their retribution, calamity and blessing follow one another; each bears it himself, and there is none to take his place. The reckoning is natural, answering to what one has done; calamity and guilt pursue the life, with no release. The good person doing good passes from joy to joy, from light to light; the evil person doing evil passes from suffering to suffering, from darkness to darkness. Who can know this? Only a Buddha knows. They teach and reveal it, but few believe and accept; birth and death do not cease, and the evil paths are not emptied. Such worldly people are hard to exhaust in full; hence there are naturally the three evil paths, with immeasurable suffering. Turning and turning within them, life after life, kalpa after kalpa, they have no time of escape, and it is hard to be freed. The pain is beyond words. This is the fifth great evil, fifth pain, fifth burning—toil and suffering like this. It is like a great fire burning a person’s body. If one can, amid it, single-mindedly control the mind, make the body upright and mindfulness correct, make words and deeds accord, do all with utmost sincerity, speak as one speaks, with mind and mouth not turning apart, do good alone and not do evil, then one alone is freed, gains the merit and blessing of the way of long life in the world, in heaven, and nirvana—this is the fifth great good.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “I tell you all: the five evils of this world are toil and suffering like this. The five pains and five burnings give rise to one another; people only do all manner of evil and do not cultivate the roots of goodness, and all naturally enter the evil destinies. Or in this present life they first suffer calamity and sickness, unable to seek death and unable to seek life—the summons of their own sins, shown to all. When the body dies they follow their deeds and enter the three evil paths, with immeasurable bitter poison, each burning itself; and after long ages they together form knots of enmity, from the smallest beginning growing into great evil. All this comes from greed for wealth and lust, from being unable to give, pressed on by delusion and desire, following the thoughts of the mind; the bonds of affliction have no release. Enriching themselves and contending for gain, they take no account of anything. Wealth, honor, and glory give present pleasure; they cannot endure insult, nor attend to cultivating goodness. Their power and influence are but little, and soon wear away. The body sits in toil and suffering, and after long ages it is greatly worse. The way of Heaven stretches and draws tight, naturally correcting and indicting; the net of its guiding cords above and below answers one another, and lonely and fearful the rich enter into it. This has been so in every age—how painful, how pitiable!”

The Buddha said to Maitreya: “The world is like this, and the Buddhas pity it all. By the power of their majestic spirit they destroy all evil and lead all to goodness. Abandon what you have in mind; receive and keep the sutras and precepts, accept and practice the way of Dharma, without transgression or loss, and at the end you will attain the way of long life in the world and nirvana.”

The Buddha said: “You devas and humans now, and the people of later ages, who receive the Buddha’s sutra words, should think on them deeply and be able to set your minds upright and your conduct correct. Let rulers do good and lead and transform those below them, each in turn commanding one another, each keeping himself upright. Revere the sages, honor the good, be kind and compassionate, broad in love. Toward the Buddha’s words of teaching and admonition, dare not be remiss. You should seek deliverance from the world and cut off the root of all the evils of birth and death; you should leave the three evil paths and their immeasurable hosts of grief, fear, and bitter pain. In this you should broadly plant the roots of virtue, bestow kindness and give gifts, and not transgress the prohibitions of the Way. Be patient and diligent, single-minded and wise. Teach and transform one another, establish virtue and do good. With mind upright and thought correct, pure in fasting and precepts, one day and one night surpass a hundred years of doing good in the Land of Immeasurable Life. Why is that? In that Buddha’s land all is actionless and natural, all accumulate manifold goodness, without a hair’s breadth of evil. Here, cultivating goodness for ten days and ten nights surpasses a thousand years of doing good in the Buddha-lands of other directions. Why is that? In the Buddha-lands of other directions, those who do good are many and those who do evil are few; merit and blessing come naturally, and there is no ground for doing evil. Only here is there much evil and nothing natural; in toil and suffering people pursue desire, deceiving and cheating one another, mind toiling and body weary, drinking bitterness and eating poison; in such evil business they never once rest.

I pity you and all the hosts of devas and humans, and with a bitter heart instruct and enlighten you, teaching you to cultivate goodness. According to what is fitting I guide you and bestow on you the sutras and Dharma; let none fail to receive and use them. According to the wishes of your minds, I lead you all to attain the Way. Wherever the Buddha has walked—in countries, towns, and villages—none fails to receive his transformation. The world is harmonious and compliant, sun and moon clear and bright. Wind and rain come in season, and pestilence does not arise. The country is rich and the people at peace, weapons of war are of no use. Virtue is honored, benevolence is raised, and all attend to cultivating propriety and yielding.”

The Buddha said: “I pity you devas and humans more than a father and mother think on their children. Now I have become Buddha in this world, subduing and transforming the five evils, dissolving the five pains, and utterly extinguishing the five burnings, attacking evil with good and pulling out the suffering of birth and death. I lead people to gain the five virtues and rise to the peace of actionlessness. After I pass away, the way of the sutras will gradually perish, people will be flattering and false, and again do all manner of evil. The five burnings and five pains will return as before. After long ages it will grow worse, beyond all telling; I have spoken of it only in brief for you.”

The Buddha said to Maitreya: “Each of you should ponder this well and teach and admonish one another; according to the Buddha’s sutras and Dharma, let none transgress.” Then Maitreya Bodhisattva, joining his palms, said: “What the Buddha has spoken is most good; the people of the world are indeed so. The Tathagata in universal compassion pities and grieves for them and leads them all to deliverance; receiving the Buddha’s weighty instruction, we dare not transgress.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Rise, and adjust your robes; with joined palms and reverence, pay homage to Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity. The Buddhas and Tathagatas of the lands of the ten directions constantly join in praising and lauding that Buddha, who is unattached and unobstructed.”

Then Ananda rose and adjusted his robes, faced the west with upright body, reverently joined his palms, and prostrated himself with all five limbs, paying homage to Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity. He said: “World-Honored One, I wish to see that Buddha’s Land of Peace and Bliss, and the great assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers.” When he had spoken these words, at once Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, released a great radiance that illumined all the Buddha-worlds. The mountains of diamond that encircle, the king of mountains Sumeru, and all the mountains great and small—all things alike became one and the same color. It was as when the flood at the end of an aeon fills the world, and all things within are submerged and no more seen; vast and boundless, only the great water is seen. That Buddha’s radiance was likewise so. The radiance of the hearers and bodhisattvas was all concealed, and only the Buddha’s light was seen, bright and blazing. Then Ananda beheld Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, majestic in virtue like the king of mountains Sumeru, rising above all the worlds, his marks and radiance illumining all.” The four assemblies of this gathering all saw it at once; and they saw this land as well, in like manner.

Then the Buddha asked Ananda and Maitreya Bodhisattva: “Do you see all the subtle, adorned, and naturally arisen things in that land, from the ground upward to the Pure Abode Heavens?” Ananda answered: “Yes, I have seen them.”
Do you also hear Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, with his great voice proclaiming throughout all worlds to transform living beings?” Ananda answered: “Yes, I have heard it.”

Do you also see the people of that land, riding palaces of the seven treasures a hundred thousand yojanas in size, without any obstruction, going everywhere in the ten directions to make offerings to the Buddhas?” He answered: “I have seen it.”

Do you also see the womb-born among the people of that land?” He answered: “I have seen them. Those womb-born dwell in palaces of a hundred yojanas, or of five hundred yojanas, each receiving all manner of bliss within them, like the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and all of it naturally so.”

Then Maitreya Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, for what cause and what condition are the people of that land womb-born or transformationally born?” The Buddha told Maitreya: “If there are living beings who with a mind of doubt cultivate all manner of merit and vow to be born in that land, not understanding the Buddha’s wisdom, the inconceivable wisdom, the inexpressible wisdom, the broad wisdom of the Great Vehicle, the unequaled and matchless supreme and highest wisdom—toward these wisdoms they doubt and do not believe; yet they still believe in sin and blessing, cultivate the roots of goodness, and vow to be born in that land. Those living beings are born in those palaces and live five hundred years, never seeing the Buddha, never hearing the sutras and Dharma, never seeing the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers. Therefore in that land they are called womb-born. But if there are living beings who clearly believe in the Buddha’s wisdom, even to the supreme wisdom, do all manner of merit, and with a mind of faith dedicate it, those living beings are born by transformation within lotus flowers of the seven treasures, sitting cross-legged; in a moment their bodily marks and radiance, their wisdom and merit, are complete and accomplished like those of the bodhisattvas. Moreover, Maitreya, the great bodhisattvas of other directions, who set their minds on seeing Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and reverently making offerings to him and to the assemblies of bodhisattvas and hearers—those bodhisattvas, when their lives end, are born in the Land of Immeasurable Life and are born by transformation within lotus flowers of the seven treasures. Maitreya, you should know that those born by transformation do so because their wisdom is superior; while the womb-born are all without wisdom, and for five hundred years never see the Buddha, never hear the sutras and Dharma, never see the bodhisattvas and the assemblies of hearers, have no means to make offerings to the Buddha, do not know the rules of the bodhisattva Dharma, and cannot cultivate merit. You should know that such persons in former lives had no wisdom, and this is brought about by their doubt.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “Suppose a wheel-turning sage king had a prison of the seven treasures, adorned in every way, furnished with beds and hangings, hung with all manner of silk canopies. If some young princes offended the king, he would at once put them inside that prison and bind them with golden chains. Their food and drink, clothing and bedding, flowers and incense and music would be like the wheel-turning king’s own, lacking nothing. What do you think? Would those princes delight in that place?” He answered: “No. By every kind of means they would seek out some great power and wish to free themselves.” The Buddha told Maitreya: “Those living beings are likewise so. Because they doubt the Buddha’s wisdom, they are born in those palaces of the seven treasures, where there is no punishment, not even a single thought of evil. But for five hundred years they do not see the Three Jewels and cannot make offerings or cultivate the roots of goodness; this they take as suffering. Though they have other pleasures, they still do not delight in that place. If such living beings recognize their own former offense, deeply repent and reproach themselves, and seek to leave that place, they at once gain their wish and go to where Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, is, to revere and make offerings to him, and can also go everywhere to immeasurable and countless other Buddhas to cultivate all manner of merit. Maitreya, you should know that a bodhisattva who gives rise to doubt loses great benefit; therefore you should clearly believe in the unsurpassed wisdom of all the Buddhas.”

Maitreya Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, in this world how many bodhisattvas who do not regress will be born in that Buddha’s land?” The Buddha told Maitreya: “In this world there are sixty-seven koṭis of non-regressing bodhisattvas who will be born in that land. Each one of those bodhisattvas has already made offerings to countless Buddhas, and is next after Maitreya. The bodhisattvas of lesser practice, and those who cultivate but little merit, cannot be counted, and all shall be born there.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “Not only the bodhisattvas of my own realm are born in that land. The Buddha-lands of other directions are likewise so. The first Buddha there is named Far-Shining; he has a hundred and eighty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The second Buddha is named Treasure Store; he has ninety koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The third Buddha is named Immeasurable Sound; he has two hundred and twenty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The fourth Buddha is named Sweet Dew Taste; he has two hundred and fifty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The fifth Buddha is named Naga Supreme; he has fourteen koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The sixth Buddha is named Supreme Power; he has fourteen thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The seventh Buddha is named Lion; he has five hundred koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The eighth Buddha is named Radiance Beyond Defilement; he has eighty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The ninth Buddha is named Foremost Virtue; he has sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The tenth Buddha is named Mountain of Wondrous Virtue; he has sixty koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The eleventh Buddha is named King of Humans; he has ten koṭis of bodhisattvas, all of whom shall be born there. The twelfth Buddha is named Unsurpassed Flower; he has countless and incalculable assemblies of bodhisattvas, all non-regressing, wise and bold, who have already made offerings everywhere to immeasurable Buddhas, and who within seven days can gather up the firm Dharma that great beings cultivate over a hundred thousand koṭis of kalpas. All these bodhisattvas shall be born there. The thirteenth Buddha is named Fearless; he has seven hundred and ninety koṭis of great bodhisattvas, and lesser bodhisattvas and monks beyond counting, all of whom shall be born there.”

The Buddha said to Maitreya: “Not only the bodhisattvas in these fourteen Buddha-lands shall be born there; in the immeasurable Buddha-lands of the worlds of the ten directions, those who are born there are likewise so, most many and countless. Were I to tell only the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions, and of the bodhisattvas and monks born in that land, a whole day and night for a kalpa would not exhaust them; I have now spoken of them only in brief for you.”

The Buddha told Maitreya: “Whoever hears the name of that Buddha, rejoices and leaps up, even for a single thought—you should know that such a person gains great benefit: he is complete in unsurpassed merit.

Therefore, Maitreya, though a great fire filled three thousand great thousand worlds, one must pass through it to hear this sutra and Dharma, to rejoice, believe, and delight in it, to receive and keep it, read and recite it, and practice as taught. Why is that? There are many bodhisattvas who wish to hear this sutra and cannot obtain it. If there are living beings who hear this sutra, they will never regress from the unsurpassed Way. Therefore you should single-mindedly believe and receive it, keep, recite, speak, and practice it. I now for the sake of all living beings expound this sutra and Dharma, causing them to see Amitabha, the Buddha of Immeasurable Purity, and all that is in his land. What should be done, all of it may be sought; do not, after my entry into nirvana, give rise again to doubt. In ages to come, when the way of the sutras is utterly extinguished, I, in compassion and pity, shall specially preserve this sutra and keep it in the world for a hundred years. Whatever living beings meet with this sutra shall, according to the wishes of their minds, all attain deliverance.”
Maitreya’s Entrustment Passage
The Passage on Specially Preserving This Sutra

The Buddha said to Maitreya: “The Tathagata’s arising in the world is hard to meet and hard to see; the sutras and the way of the Buddhas are hard to obtain and hard to hear; the supreme Dharma of the bodhisattvas and the paramitas are also hard to hear; and to meet a good teacher and, hearing the Dharma, be able to practice it—this too is hard. But to hear this sutra and with faith and delight receive and keep it is the hardest of the hard; nothing surpasses this difficulty. Therefore my Dharma is thus made, thus spoken, thus taught. You should believe and comply, and practice according to the Dharma.”

Then when the World-Honored One had spoken this sutra and Dharma, immeasurable living beings all brought forth the mind of unsurpassed right enlightenment. Twelve thousand nayutas of people attained the pure Dharma-eye. Twenty-two koṭis of devas and humans attained the fruit of non-returning. Eight hundred thousand monks exhausted their outflows and their minds were freed. Four koṭis of bodhisattvas attained non-regression. Adorning themselves with the merit of their great vows, in future ages they shall accomplish right enlightenment. Then the three thousand great thousand worlds shook in six ways, and a great light shone throughout the lands of the ten directions; hundreds of thousands of musics arose of themselves, and immeasurable wondrous flowers fell in profusion.

When the Buddha had finished speaking the sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva and the assemblies of bodhisattvas who had come from the ten directions, the Elder Ananda, the great hearers, and all the great assembly, hearing what the Buddha had spoken, none failed to rejoice.
Translated by decree by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Great Tang
The Great Jewel Heap Sutra, Scroll Seventeen: The Gathering of Amitabha Tathagata

blocks.text: The Gathering of Amitabha Tathagata, Part One

inline.s: Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha dwelt on Vulture Peak in Rajagriha, together with a great assembly of monks, twelve thousand in all, all great hearers known and recognized by the many. Their names were: the Venerable Ajñata-Kauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahānāma, Bhadrika, Vimala, Subhadra, Sampūrṇakīrti, Gavāṃpati, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Nadī-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, Mahā-Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahā-Maudgalyāyana, Mahā-Kātyāyana, Mahā-Kapphina, Mahā-Cunda, Pūrṇa-Maitrāyaṇīputra, Aniruddha, Revata, Upananda, Kapphiṇa, Nanda, Svāgata, Rāhula, Ānanda, and others, with these as foremost.

There were also assemblies of great bodhisattvas, namely Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and the assemblies of great bodhisattvas of the present Bhadra kalpa, surrounding him before and behind.

He was also accompanied by the assembly of sixteen good men including Bhadrapāla, namely the Bodhisattva Good Thought on Meaning, the Bodhisattva Wisdom and Eloquence, the Bodhisattva Contemplating Non-Abiding, the Bodhisattva Skillful in Transforming Spiritual Powers, the Bodhisattva Light Banner, the Bodhisattva Supreme Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Stillness of Faculties, the Bodhisattva Wisdom Vow, the Bodhisattva Fragrant Elephant, the Bodhisattva Jewel Banner, and others, with these as foremost.

All together they cultivated the way of Samantabhadra, fulfilled all the practices and vows of a bodhisattva, and dwelt at peace in all dharmas of merit, reaching the Buddha-Dharma and the ultimate other shore. They vowed to accomplish equal right enlightenment in every world. They further vowed to be born in the Tushita Heaven, and when their lives there ended, to descend and be born from the right side, to walk seven steps, to release a great radiance that illumined all Buddha-worlds and shook them in six ways, and to proclaim: “I am the most honored in all the world.” All the devas of Brahma and Indra came to attend him in person. They further manifested learning writing and calculation, calendrical science, grammar, the arts and crafts, medicine, the nurturing of life, and talismans and seals, and in other games and sports they excelled above others. Dwelling in the royal palace, they wearied of the realms of desire; seeing old age, sickness, and death, they awakened to the impermanence of the world. They gave up the royal throne, crossed the city wall, and went forth to study the Way. They removed all their ornaments and the kāśika cloth, put on the monastic robe, and practiced austerities for six years. They were able to make such a display in the lands of the five turbidities. Conforming to the world, they bathed in the Nairañjanā River and went toward the site of enlightenment. The naga kings welcomed and praised them; the assemblies of bodhisattvas circumambulated them to the right and sang their praises. Then the bodhisattva accepted grass, spread it himself beneath the bodhi tree, and sat cross-legged. They further saw the hosts of Mara gather around and prepare to do harm. By the power of concentration and wisdom the bodhisattva subdued the hosts of Mara and accomplished unsurpassed enlightenment. Brahma the king urged them and they turned the wheel of Dharma. Bold and fearless, their Buddha-voice roared like thunder; they beat the Dharma-drum and blew the Dharma-conch. They raised the great Dharma-banner and lit the torch of right Dharma. They embraced the right Dharma and all the meditative concentrations. They rained the great Dharma-rain, moistening and enriching living beings. They shook the great Dharma-thunder, awakening all. A great light shone throughout all Buddha-lands. Within those worlds the earth all trembled. The palaces of Mara were destroyed, and Papiyas was terrified. They broke down the city of afflictions and cast off the net of views. Far from black dharmas, they gave rise to white dharmas. They could receive and digest the food offered to a Buddha. To tame living beings they proclaimed the wondrous principle. Sometimes they showed a smile and released hundreds of thousands of rays. They ascended the stage of consecration and received the bodhi prophecy. Sometimes they accomplished the Buddha-way, and were seen to enter nirvana. They caused immeasurable sentient beings all to attain the extinction of outflows, and matured bodhisattvas in boundless roots of goodness. In all such Buddha-lands they could manifest. It is like a magician skilled in the art of illusion, able to manifest the forms of men and women; yet within those forms nothing at all can be grasped. Just so, those bodhisattvas, because they have well learned the merit of boundless illusion, can manifest transformations in accord, and because they well understand the way of transformation, they manifest all Buddha-lands and reveal great compassion. Benefiting all living beings everywhere, they fulfill the vows and practices of a bodhisattva. They accomplish boundless and immeasurable gates of meaning. They penetrate the equal and all-good dharmas and are complete in their cultivation. Into all Buddha-lands they enter equally. They are constantly urged on and empowered by all Buddhas, and all Tathagatas know, recognize, and approve them. To teach bodhisattvas they act as ācāryas, constantly practicing the corresponding boundless practices. They penetrate the conduct of all Dharma-realms and well understand sentient beings and lands; they also constantly aspire to make offerings to all Tathagatas. They see all manner of bodies as like reflections. Well learning Indra’s net, they can break the net of Mara. They destroy the net of views and enter the net of sentient beings. They can transcend the retinue of afflictions and the companions and people of Mara. Far beyond the stages of hearers and pratyekabuddhas, they enter the Dharma-gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and can abide in skillful means. They never delight in entering the nirvana of the two vehicles, but attain the samadhis of non-arising and non-ceasing, and gain all dhāraṇī-gates. Their faculties are broad and great, their eloquence decisive. In the bodhisattva-piṭaka dharmas they are well able to understand. The Buddha-flower samadhi they enter at will. They are complete in all kinds of profound meditative concentration. All Buddhas appear before them, and in a single thought they travel throughout Buddha-lands and return, no different in time. In what is hard and what is not hard they can understand all extremes. They expound the ultimate reality and well understand its distinctions. They gain the Buddha’s eloquence and dwell in the practice of Samantabhadra. They are well able to distinguish the languages of living beings and surpass all worldly dharmas; they well understand all supramundane dharmas. They gain the perfection of sovereign mastery over requisites and bear living beings, as a friend not asked. They can hold the Dharma-treasury of all Tathagatas and dwell in it without interruption, keeping the lineage of all Buddhas. Pitying living beings, they can open the Dharma-eye. They close the evil destinies and open the door to good destinies. Beholding all living beings, they can form the thought of father, mother, and brother; and again they regard living beings as they regard their own bodies. Having realized the perfection of all praised virtues, they well understand and praise all the virtues of the Tathagatas, together with the rest of the dharmas of praise and virtue. Thus the assembly of such great bodhisattvas, immeasurable and boundless, all came together.

Then the Venerable Ananda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: “Great Virtue, World-Honored One, your bodily form and all your faculties are utterly pure; your majestic light blazes like molten gold, and like a bright mirror it gathers and reflects radiance. From ages past until now I have never once seen such a sight; I am glad to behold it and give rise to a rare thought. The World-Honored One now enters the great stillness of samadhi, practices the Tathagata’s practices, all of them complete, and well establishes the practice of a great being. Pondering the Buddhas of past, future, and present—why, World-Honored One, do you dwell in this mindfulness?”
Then the Buddha said to Ananda: “How now are you able to know this meaning? Did some devas come and tell you? Or is it because you have seen me and know it yourself?”
Ananda said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I saw the Tathagata’s rare radiance, and so gave rise to this thought; it was not because of devas or others.”

The Buddha told Ananda: “Excellent, excellent! Your question now is well asked. You are able to observe the subtle and wondrous eloquence and to ask the Tathagata such a meaning. It is for the sake of all Tathagatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and of those who dwell in great compassion to benefit living beings, who are rare great beings like the udumbara flower appearing in the world, that you ask this meaning. And again, for the sake of pitying and benefiting all living beings, you are able to ask the Tathagata such a meaning. Ananda, the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is well able to reveal immeasurable knowledge and vision. Why is that? The Tathagata’s knowledge and vision have no obstruction. Ananda, if the Tathagata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, wished to remain in the world, he could in the time of a meal remain for immeasurable and countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas. And were he to prolong it beyond that number, the Tathagata’s body and all his faculties would neither increase nor decrease. Why is that? The Tathagata has gained sovereign mastery of samadhi and has reached the other shore. In all dharmas he is supremely sovereign. Therefore, Ananda, listen well and ponder it well; I shall explain it for you in detail.”
Ananda said to the Buddha: “Yes, World-Honored One, I wish and long to hear it!”

Then the Buddha told Ananda: “In ages past, beyond asaṃkhyeyas and countless great kalpas, a Buddha appeared named Dipankara. Long before that Buddha, beyond measure, there was a Buddha named Austerity who arose in the world. Before the Buddha Austerity there was again a Tathagata named Moon Face. Before the Buddha Moon Face, beyond measure, there was the Buddha Sandalwood Fragrance, and before that Buddha the Buddha Sumeru Heap. Before the Buddha Heap there was again the Buddha Wondrous Height Kalpa. And so in turn there were the Buddha Face Beyond Defilement, the Buddha Undefiled, the Buddha Naga Deva, the Buddha King of Mountain Sound, the Buddha Sumeru Heap, the Buddha Golden Store, the Buddha Illuminating Radiance, the Buddha Radiance Sovereign, the Buddha Lineage of the Great Earth, the Buddha Blazing Radiance of Vaiḍūrya Gold Light, the Buddha Moon Image, the Buddha Opening Flowers Adorned with Light, the Buddha Wondrous Sea of Supreme Enlightenment Sporting in Spiritual Powers, the Buddha Diamond Light, the Buddha Great Agada Fragrant Light, the Buddha Mind Beyond Affliction, the Buddha Increase of Treasures, the Buddha Bold Heap, the Buddha Supreme Heap, the Buddha Upholding the Great Merit of Dharma-gift and Spiritual Powers, the Buddha Outshining Sun and Moon, the Buddha Illuminating Vaiḍūrya, the Buddha Mind-Awakening Flower, the Buddha Moonlight, the Buddha Sunlight, the Buddha King of Flower Garland Colors Opening Spiritual Powers, the Buddha Water Moonlight, the Buddha Destroyer of the Darkness of Ignorance, the Buddha Canopy of Pearl and Coral, the Buddha Tisya, the Buddha Supreme Flower, the Buddha Roar of Dharma Wisdom, the Buddha with Lion’s Roar and Goose and Swan Voice, and the Buddha Brahma Voice Naga Roar. Such Buddhas arose in the world, each separated from the next by kalpas beyond measure. Before the Buddha Naga Roar appeared in the world, in countless kalpas before, there was the Buddha World Sovereign. Before the Buddha World Sovereign, in boundless kalpas, a Buddha appeared in the world named the Tathagata King of Freedom in the World, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Perfect in Wisdom and Conduct, Well-Gone, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Beings, Teacher of Devas and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. Ananda, in that Buddha’s Dharma there was a monk named Dharmakara, who had surpassing vows and practices, and whose powers of mindfulness and wisdom were heightened. His mind was firm and unmoved, his merit and wisdom surpassing, his human form dignified. Ananda, that monk Dharmakara went to where the Tathagata King of Freedom in the World was, bared his right shoulder, bowed his head to the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse:
The Tathagata’s light is immeasurable and boundless; throughout the world no light can compare.
All the suns, moons, and maṇi jewels are outshone by the Buddha’s majestic light.
The World-Honored One can utter a single sound, and each living being understands it according to its kind.
He can also manifest a single wondrous body, and cause all beings to see it according to their kind.
In precepts, concentration, wisdom, diligence, and much hearing, no living being can equal him.
The stream of his mind’s awakened wisdom is like the great sea; he well understands the most profound Dharma.
Delusions exhausted and faults gone, he is worthy of offerings; such is his sacred virtue—he alone is the World-Honored One.
The Buddha has a surpassing and mighty radiance that illumines immeasurable lands of the ten directions.
I now praise all his virtues, hoping for blessing and wisdom equal to the Tathagata’s.
He can save all the worlds from the many sorrows of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
May I dwell in samadhi and expound the Dharma-gates of giving and precepts.
With patience, diligence, concentration, and wisdom, may I become a Buddha and save living beings.
To seek the unsurpassed great bodhi, I make offerings to all the wondrously awakened of the ten directions.
Hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas, as many as the sands of the Ganges.
And may I gain a great spiritual radiance, doubling its shining over koṭis of Buddha-lands like Ganges sands.
And with boundless surpassing effort, may I attain a supreme and vast pure abode.
In such an unequaled Buddha-land I shall settle living beings and benefit them.
The supreme great beings of the ten directions shall all be born there with joyful minds.
Only the Buddha’s sacred wisdom can know and bear witness; I now seek the power of firmness.
Though I sink into all the uninterrupted hells, such a vow and mind shall never retreat.
The unobstructed wisdom of all the world should know and understand such a mind.

Moreover, Ananda, when the monk Dharmakara had praised the Buddha’s virtues, he said to the World-Honored One: “I now bring forth the mind of unsurpassed right enlightenment. I pray the Tathagata to expound such dharmas for me, that I may in the world attain the unequaled accomplishment of great bodhi and fully embrace a pure and adorned Buddha-land.”
The Buddha said to the monk: “You should cultivate for yourself a pure Buddha-land.”

Dharmakara said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I have no such power to embrace and receive them. I pray the Tathagata to tell me of the other Buddha-lands, pure and adorned; when we have heard it, we vow to perfect them.”

Then the World-Honored One broadly expounded for him the twenty-one koṭis of pure Buddha-lands in their full adornment. When he had spoken this Dharma, a koṭi of years passed. Ananda, the monk Dharmakara embraced all the pure and adorned matters within those twenty-one koṭis of Buddha-lands. Having embraced them, he fulfilled five kalpas in thought and cultivation.”
